JUDGMENT ON THE APPLICATION
FOR THE ISSUANCE OF A SAFEGUARD ORDER
:

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

This Court
is asked to decide an Application for the issuance of a safeguard order (the “
Application
”)
presented by Plaintiffs, who are comprised of students of McGill University and
duly registered members of Defendant Student Society of McGill University (“
SSMU
”).
The Impleaded party is McGill University and is not taking position today in
the matter.

[
2
]

For
reasons that follow, the Application is dismissed and the safeguard order is
not granted.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND

[
3
]

The
Application concerns a certain policy against antisemitism (the “
Policy
”)
that was drafted by Mr. Hugo-Victor Solomon (“
Solomon
”), Vice President
External of the SSMU, in September 2024.

[
4
]

The
Policy was the object of a vote taken December 5, 2024, which Plaintiffs
initially alleged was in violation of the SSMU's constitution and bylaws. They
filed on December 8, 2024 an
Originating Application for Declaratory
Judgment and for the Issuance of Provisional, Interlocutory and Permanent
Injunctive Relief
(later modified on December 28, 2024).

[
5
]

On December
9, 2024, the Honourable Justice Daniel Urbas granted Plaintiffs’ request for
provisional interlocutory injunction and rendered an order notably issuing a
provisional interlocutory injunction to be valid for a period of ten days
whereby Defendant SSMU, its officers, directors, agents, assigns and employees
were to suspend the vote by their board of directors ratifying the SSMU Policy
Against Antisemitism 2024-11- 07 (which was adopted by motion on December 5,
2024 at the meeting of the SSMU Legislative Committee) (the “
December 9
Order
”).

[
6
]

Justice
Urbas found that Plaintiffs, in their respective capacities, were entitled to
participate in the activities of the SSMU, according to the rules by which they
abide. Plaintiffs had alleged that there had been a breach of due process in
giving them adequate notice of the reconsideration of a vote that had failed in
November after due consideration. Justice Urbas held that the lack of notice
was not justified on the factual record, and that there had been no adequate
notice to prepare for, and participate in, the meeting in December.

[
7
]

On
December 17, 2024, Plaintiffs filed an Application for a Safeguard Order
renewing the December 9 Order.

[
8
]

When
Defendant later confirmed that they had no declared intention to ratify the
Policy at their next scheduled board of directors meeting on January 7th, 2025,
Plaintiffs decided not to renew the Provisional Injunction issued by Justice
Urbas.

[
9
]

On
February 12th, 2025, the SSMU’s attorney confirmed that the Policy would be
placed on the agenda of their board of directors meeting of March 11th, 2025.

[
10
]

On February 26th, 2025,
Plaintiffs notified and filed a
Modified Application for the Issuance of a
Safeguard Order
, to be effective for a period of six months to safeguard
their rights pending adjudication on the merits.

[
11
]

On March 5th, 2025, the
Honourable Justice Bernard Larocque granted Plaintiffs’ Modified Application
for Safeguard Order and rendered a Safeguard Order to be in force for a maximal
period of six months, subject to additional renewal, ordering Defendant and its
officers, directors, agents, assigns and employees to suspend the vote by its
board of directors ratifying the Policy (the “
March 6 Order
”). Justice
Larocque reasoned that Justice Urbas’ reasons were still valid and that the
situation had not changed since December 9
th
. He ratified his
reasons.

[
12
]

The parties were summoned
for a case management conference to determine the scheduling of the preliminary
procedural steps required to ready the present matter for trial readiness, and
in this regard, the Honourable Éric Dufour rendered several case management
orders on March 17
th
and March 20
th
, 2025.

[
13
]

In the interim, on April 3
rd
,
2025, Defendant petitioned the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal the Larocque
Judgment, as appears from the Court Record. The leave to appeal is presentable
on May 1
st
, 2025.

[
14
]

The file is currently
suspended until April 16
th
, 2025, date of the next scheduled case
management conference, as per the Judgment of the Honourable Éric Dufour on
March 20th, 2025.

[
15
]

On March 19
th
,
2025, Solomon sent an email to Defendant’s members, informing them that the
Policy would be tabled anew before the Defendant’s Legislative Council the
following evening and that a full debate on the Policy would take place two weeks
later – on April 3rd, 2025 – before the Defendant’s Legislative Councillors.

[
16
]

The Policy enclosed in the
notice sent by Solomon is a revised version of the initial version that was the
subject of the December 9
th
and March 5
th
orders.

[
17
]

On March 28
th
,
2025, several of the Plaintiffs issued a joint reply to Solomon in order to:
(i) express their dissent with the newest attempt to force passage of the
Policy without having provided for proper and meaningful consultation prior to
its drafting; and (ii) warn Defendant that the passage of the Policy would only
cause further harm to the Jewish student community.

[
18
]

On April 3
rd
,
2025, Defendant submitted the Policy to its Legislative Council, who voted to
approve same for it to be sent to Defendant’s board of directors for
ratification.

[
19
]

The Defendant’s board of
directors is scheduled to meet on April 8
th
, 2025, at which time the
Policy is to be submitted for ratification.

[
20
]

On April 7
th
,
2025, Plaintiffs filed an
Application for the Issuance of a Safeguard Order

asking to suspend immediately the vote by the Defendant’s board of directors
ratifying the SSMU Policy Against Antisemitism 2025-04-03, which was adopted by
motion on April 3
rd
, 2025 at the SSMU Legislative Committee meeting.

[
21
]

The Court is asked to
decide this safeguard application.

[
22
]

In their Application for a
Safeguard, the Plaintiffs assert that the Policy at stake “touches directly on
their rights to freely express their identities and to be treated as equal
members of the McGill student community”, and that the content of the Policy
“risks having a nefarious impact on the Jewish students at McGill University”.
They add that “Defendant’s persistent and intentional omission and/or refusal
to ensure proper and meaningful consultation prior to seeking to adopt and ratify
the
[
Policy
]
, as is required pursuant to s. 5.1
of Defendant’s Consultation Policy
[…]
not only undermines any credence to the impugned process, but
also is illustrative that Defendant is acting in bad faith and with the intent
to harm Plaintiffs by disregarding their legitimate expectations and rights as
an affected stakeholder group, the whole in contravention of sections 6 & 7
of the
Civil Code of Quebec

[…]”.

[
23
]

While Plaintiffs consider
that this Court should decide the Application considering the two previous
orders, Defendant argues that this Application is distinguishable because it is
founded on a different Policy than the one subject of the previous orders,
given that the initial Policy was subject to several changes and amendments
since November 2024. Defendant further adds that the previous orders were not
based, as is the case here, on the lack of appropriate consultation of the
Plaintiffs. The parties, accordingly, do not consent in any way to considering
this instance as a renewal of Justice Larocque’s March 5, 2025 Safeguard Order.

[
24
]

Indeed, the December 9
Order suspends the vote ratifying the SSMU Policy Against Antisemitism
2024-11-07, the March 5 Order suspends the same vote ratifying the SSMU Policy
Against Antisemitism 2024-11-07, and the present safeguard order seeks to
suspend the vote ratifying the SSMU Policy Against Antisemitism 2025-04-03.

[
25
]

Because the present
Application for a Safeguard Order is based on a revised version of the Policy,
and because there are new facts, the Court is not sitting in review of the
March 5 Order and must proceed
de novo
[1]

and decide whether to issue a new safeguard order.

[
26
]

The normal tests for the
granting of a safeguard order must then be applied.

ANALYSIS

APPLICABLE LAW

[
27
]

The Court of Appeal
recently summarized the law applicable to safeguard orders
[2]
:

“
[
27
]
Based on well-established
precedent, a safeguard order is [translation] “a discretionary judicial
measure, issued for conservatory purposes, in an emergency situation, for a
limited period and in a matter in which the respondent has not yet been able to
present all its grounds”. It is a provisional and temporary measure that does
not rule on the parties’ rights. It is designed to prevent the loss of rights
or the creation of a situation that weakens or destroys the balance between the
parties.

[28] Safeguard orders are akin to
provisional injunctions because, in the same manner as the latter, their
[translation] “purpose is to preserve the status quo pending the hearing on the
merits, thereby ensuring that the judgment is not rendered in vain”. They must
therefore satisfy the same criteria – namely, appearance of right, serious or
irreparable harm, the balance of convenience, and urgency.

[…]

[30] In the new Code of Civil
Procedure, the power of courts to issue safeguard orders is set out in art. 49
(general powers) and art. 158 (case management measures).

[31] Article 49 C.C.P. states the
general principle that, in all matters and at any stage of proceedings, courts
and judges may, even on their own initiative, grant injunctions or issue orders
to safeguard the parties’ rights, including in situations for which no solution
is provided by law. As for art. 158 C.C.P., it confers the specific power on
courts to issue safeguard orders, effective for not more than six months, as a
case management measure
[
…
]

[32] Article 158 C.C.P. is considered
to be a variant of art. 49 C.C.P.; it [translation] “does not completely
exhaust the latter’s field”. As decided in
Limouzin c. Side City Studios Inc
.,
in injunction matters, safeguard orders are a case management tool
[translation] “whose sole purpose is to allow the parties to quickly progress
from the provisional injunction stage to the interlocutory stage”. And while
the legislature may not have reproduced art. 754.2 f.C.C.P. in the chapter on
injunctions, the case law on this provision is still applicable: [translation]
“The way in which it is to be used remains the same […], it must be a
short-term order serving as a bridge to the interlocutory stage”.

[33] Lastly, a safeguard order should
not be the equivalent of a judgment on the merits, nor should its scope be such
that it effectively seals the fate of the dispute.
[3]
"

[References omitted]

[
28
]

Accordingly, Plaintiffs
must satisfy the same criteria as those required for the issuance of a
provisional interlocutory injunction; namely: (i) that they have an appearance
of right to the redress sought; (ii) that they will suffer serious or
irreparable harm if the redress sought is not granted; (iii) that the balance of
inconveniences leans in their favour; and (iv) that there is urgency that said
injunctive relief be granted on a provisional basis.

[
29
]

Based on the following
reasons, the Court finds that Plaintiffs have failed to fulfil their burden to
establish those criteria and accordingly, the Application for the Issuance of a
Safeguard Order must fail.

APPLICATION TO THE FACTS OF THE CASE

[
30
]

Concerning the condition
of
urgency
, it requires both that a prejudicial event is more or less
imminent, and that the petitioner has acted with all due dispatch in bringing
the matter before the courts.

[
31
]

In this case, the
ratification of the Policy has been added to Defendant’s Board of Directors
meeting Agenda for April 8
th
, 2025. Thus, it is indeed imperative
that the Court intervene to assert the suspension of the ratification of the
Policy pending a decision on its validity on the merits. Plaintiffs have
brought this matter forward in a timely manner. This criterion is thus met.
However, it must be noted here that the urgency originates from the Defendant’s
decision to hold the meeting quickly. In any event, the Court will examine the
other criteria.

[
32
]

Importantly,
Appearance
of right
has not been demonstrated.

[
33
]

Plaintiffs argue that no
“clear and meaningful efforts” were made by Defendant to consult Plaintiffs
with respect to the Policy, whether in respect to its first, second or third
introduction. In support of this argument is Rabbi Shmuly Weiss’ affidavit, in
which he outlines the consultation process in respect of the 2018 version of
Defendant’s Policy against Antisemitism, and the difference in the level of
consultation that was then provided, in comparison with the present matter.

[
34
]

This argument should be
set aside. Suggesting that the consultation process should, in this case, be
identical to a process followed in 2018, at a time when the Policy had not yet
been enacted, is unconvincing. There was indeed a temporary one-year Motion
regarding antisemitism in 2018, but it was never renewed nor fully implemented,
as appears from Exhibit R-9.

[
35
]

The Court must specify
here that in examining the appearance of right, evidence specifying facts that
occurred at the time the Policy was initially drafted and starting to be
discussed is relevant to understanding how the Policy was developed and the
extent of the consultation process that was followed. Therefore, even if the
vote at stake in this safeguard application is based on a different version of
the Policy, to understand the consultation process, one must not only consider
the consultations having been held since the latest version of the Policy was
circulated on March 19
th
, 2025. As indicated in the March 19
th

email in Exhibit R-6, feedback from various groups was considered, as well as
open letters and email consultations. The SSMU thereafter implemented several
changes to the Policy to reflect the input received from members.

[
36
]

Furthermore, the
consultation process to be followed must be contemporary to the Policy being
voted on and enacted. In this case, a lengthy consultation process appears to
have been followed by the SSMU, as described at length by Solomon in his
affidavit. Indeed, Solomon explains that all members of the SSMU, as well as
specific self-identifying Jewish groups, were invited by email to take part in
the consultation and had the occasion to provide feedback throughout September
2024. In addition, all members of the SSMU were provided the opportunity to ask
questions at the Fall General Assembly, on September 30
th
, 2024.
They were also provided an opportunity to speak and participate in the
consultation process regarding the Policy at the question and debate periods at
the Legislative Council's meetings on November 7
th
, 2024, and
November 21
st
, 2024. Solomon explains that on both occasions, the
Policy was extensively debated and discussed.

[
37
]

On October 22
nd
,
2024, Solomon explains that considering the consultation process to be
satisfactory, the Steering Committee allowed the motion to adopt the Policy to
be presented as a Notice of Motion of Councillors on October 24
th
, 2024
(Exhibit HVS-10A). Then, as Notice of Motion had been provided, the Steering
Committee allowed the Policy to be presented as a main motion for debate and
vote at the next Legislative Council meeting of November 7
th
, 2024
(Exhibit HVS-10B).

[
38
]

Paragraphs 14 to 37 of
Solomon’s Affidavit precisely describe the process followed for consultations
until October 24
th
, 2024, when the Steering Committee moved for the
Policy to be presented to the Legislative Council for notice of motion.

[
39
]

On November 7
th
,
2024, Councillors, gallery members, and stakeholders debated and discussed the
Policy for two hours.

[
40
]

According to Solomon’s
affidavit, at the Legislative Council meeting on November 21
st
,
2024, approximately seventy SSMU members attended as non-voting gallery members,
including many stakeholders from the SSMU's Jewish community, both in support
of and against the Policy Against Antisemitism, and the Policy was debated
extensively over two and a half hours.

[
41
]

As Solomon explains in his
Exhibit R-6 March 19
th
, 2025 email to executives of the Jewish
Student Groups at McGill, opportunities were provided to comment on the
previous version of the Policy and on the “latest version” of the Policy at the
legislative council meeting. He then reminded members that a full debate and
vote would take place on April 3
rd
, and that they were encouraged to
attend and participate in the debate before the legislative councillors proceed
to vote. He added that until then, group members were encouraged to reach out
to him with questions, proposed amendments or additional feedback regarding the
Policy.

[
42
]

The Notice of Motion
Regarding the SSMU Policy Against Antisemitism 2025-04-03, in Exhibit R-7,
details all consultations that were completed in relation to the Policy at
pages 4, 5 and 6. Precisely, consultations with Jewish student groups are
detailed at pages 5 and 6. At page 6 is a bullet point notably stating that the
concerns raised by Hillel McGill were “expressly integrated into the current
version of the document in light of the candid feedback communicated by
Hillel.” Those pages evidence a thorough and extensive consultation of the SSMU
members, and precisely, of Jewish groups at McGill.

[
43
]

Plaintiffs submit that the
“clear and meaningful efforts” made by Defendant to consult them with respect
to a third attempt to pass the Policy were limited to requesting feedback by
e-mail on a policy that had already been pre-drafted and approved by
Defendant’s legal counsel and had been suspended judicially twice. This
argument is unconvincing, given the extent of the consultations described by
Solomon to have taken place.

[
44
]

The evidence shows that
Solomon contacted the Chabad House to obtain comments and participation on the
Policy’s drafting (as per exhibit SB-3). On September 28
th
, 2024,
the Chabad at McGill Executive Board clearly stated that it was their last
communication with Solomon. No further communication or consultation with this
group was to be initiated or accepted. Chabad House Chabad McGill is a
Plaintiff in the present matter. It cannot now complain of not being consulted
when it was invited to and declined to participate.

[
45
]

It is true, as Plaintiffs
note, that the notion of “clear and meaningful efforts” is addressed in Section
7.4 of Defendant’s Consultation Policy (filed as Exhibit P-7). However, this
Section merely lists situations or contexts in which an appropriate level of
consultation is considered to have been met, such as when those eligible to
vote on a motion are timely communicated with and provided documentation about
the vote, or whereby forums of opportunities to allow relevant stakeholders to
submit statements for consideration by the governing body are provided. It
provides a list of best practices for consultations but does not set firm rules
in that regard.

[
46
]

In addition, there were
communications with interested groups about the Policy, and those groups were
repeatedly invited to participate and submit comments on the Policy. Forum of
opportunities were indeed provided to be consulted and to participate in
consultations.

[
47
]

In addition, Section 3.2.
of the SSMU Consultation Policy defines "consultation" as a dialogue
and exchange of views between the individual leading the consultation process
and stakeholders, conducted in a manner that allows stakeholders to express
opinions or provide recommendations based on the information shared regarding
the proposed measures. The evidence shows that this is how the consultations
were held here.

[
48
]

In fact, even if the
Consultation Policy does not indicate who should be consulted, as Solomon explains
in his affidavit, and as Exhibit R-7 evidences, interested groups were
consulted, and in particular, Jewish groups at McGill. The discussion appears
to have been contested, and comments were made by advocates for both sides of
adopting and rejecting the Policy.

[
49
]

Since I conclude that
appearance of right is not met, there is no need to address irreparable or
serious harm, and balance of convenience.

[
50
]

In any event, as for the
serious
or irreparable harm
, Plaintiffs allege that they will be deprived of their
right to contest the validity of the motion adopting the Policy, and that the
hostile climate at McGill risks being aggravated and/or exacerbated if the
Policy is ratified and given effect, as this “will legitimize the hate,
intimidation and harassment being suffered by McGill Students”.

[
51
]

This allegation is
unsupported by the evidence consisting of the affidavits of Rabbi Weiss and
Samuel Benzaquen. While there may well be a hostile environment currently at
McGill, the Plaintiffs have not demonstrated why or how the fact of allowing
the vote to proceed on the Policy will “legitimize the hate, intimidation and
harassment” suffered by McGill students.

[
52
]

The
balance of
convenience
, furthermore, does not favour either party.

[
53
]

Therefore, except for
urgency, the criteria to grant a safeguard order are not met.

[
54
]

Finally, Defendants ask
orally that this Court declare the Application for a Safeguard Order to be
abusive and reject the Application and/or the Originating Application and
Modified Application. They invoke Strategic Lawsuit Against Public
Participation arguments, appearing to refer, at least in part, to their pending

Motion to Dismiss Action to Terminate a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public
Participation
, filed on February 25
th
, 2025. This Motion is
currently being filtered or
triaged
by the Honorable Justice Éric
Dufour, who has been assigned as special case management judge. Accordingly, it
is not for this Court to decide the matter of abuse and a potential SLAPP
argument. This oral motion is thus deferred to Justice Éric Dufour or to the
merits stage when it can be argued and responded to properly by Plaintiffs.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
55
]

DISMISSES
the Plaintiffs’
Application for a Safeguard Order;

[
56
]

DEFERS
the Defendant’s Oral
Motion to Dismiss Due to Abuse and Action to Terminate a Strategic Lawsuit
Against Public Participation to a determination by special coordinating Justice
Éric Dufour or to the merits;

[
57
]

THE WHOLE, WITH COSTS.
